-

Sweet Potato!

-

Ranked!

-

0.1 grams of fat. Omega 3 is 5 milligrams, doing a lot of the work here. For a tuber, the cleanest win is a more stable carb profile.

-

1.6 grams of protein. Bioavailability is 35%, one of the best parts of the protein story. Protein is usually limited here, so the other sections have to carry more.

-

Vitamin a at 160% daily value stands out most. That is major vitamin support.

-

Potassium at 10% daily value stands out most. Useful, but still pretty limited.

-

On the plus side: carotenoid content gives it extra value. That adds a useful plant-pigment angle beyond the basic carb role most tubers play. Fairly filling for the calories. Heavy added fats or sugary toppings can change the practical outcome. Protein contribution is light. Like most tubers, it is not doing much in the protein lane.

-

Sweet Potato has a genuinely strong overall case. The practical downsides are real, but they do not outweigh the upside. Best when you want practical carbs and the rest of the profile is still reasonably clean.

-

episode.narrationText:
Zucchini!

-

Ranked!

-

0.3 grams of fat. Omega 3 is 15 milligrams, doing a lot of the work here. For a vegetable, this is all about actual nutritional payoff.

-

Glycemic index is 15 GI. 3.1 grams of carbs. Glycemic index, fibre, and sugar are doing most of the work. For vegetables, low downside is useful, but there still needs to be real payoff.

-

1.2 grams of protein. Bioavailability is 35%, one of the best parts of the protein story. Protein is not the main pitch here, but extra support still matters.

-

Vitamin c at 20% daily value stands out most. That is only mild support overall.

-

Minerals are basically not part of the case here.

-

Pros first: good volume for the calories. That matters for satiety and general usefulness. Helps add volume without much calorie cost. That makes vegetables easier to use often. Easy to build meals around. A practical plus because good foods need realistic use cases.

-

Now the downsides: rarely carries a meal by itself. That is normal here, but still part of the tradeoff. Usually needs pairing to make a full meal. Most vegetables are not complete by themselves. Energy density is very low. Good for some use cases, but not enough on its own.

-

Zucchini does have a few real-world upsides. But the nutrition case is still weak and the downsides drag it down hard. Best only when you need a low-commitment add-on rather than a nutrient-dense anchor.

-

C tier.
